pathway.title: Programming
pathway.description: Build clear, maintainable software by progressing from Python foundations to modular design, data boundaries, testing, and integration.

course.title: Python Programming — Intermediate
course.short_description: An intermediate Python course focused on maintainable program design, generators, classes, data boundaries, testing, debugging, and small offline applications.
course.prerequisites: Completion of Python Programming — Beginner or equivalent ability with variables, conditions, loops, collections, functions, and basic error handling.
learning_outcomes: Structure Python code into modules with clear interfaces and expressive iteration.
Model behavior with classes, dataclasses, composition, protocols, and honest type hints.
Read and write structured data while managing files, resources, and domain-specific failures safely.
Build deterministic tests, debug from evidence, and use responsible logging.
Integrate a small maintainable offline application with documented boundaries and privacy limits.
course.dependencies: Python 3.10+ standard library only; no third-party packages required.

modules.title: Design expressive Python programs
modules.description: Structure intermediate code with modules, comprehensions, and lazy iteration.

topics.title: Design maintainable programs with modules and interfaces
topics.description: Intermediate programs become easier to change when related responsibilities are separated.

lesson.title: Design maintainable programs with modules and interfaces
objectives: Explain why a larger program benefits from separation into modules.
Create a small module and import a function from it.
Describe an interface as the names, inputs, outputs, and assumptions a component exposes.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Intermediate programs become easier to change when related responsibilities are separated. A module is a Python file that groups definitions such as functions, constants, and classes. Importing a module lets another file use that code through a clear interface rather than copying it. A useful interface tells callers the function name, expected argument types, return value, and important failure behavior. Keep the public surface small: if callers depend on every internal detail, refactoring becomes risky. Python executes a module's top-level statements when it is first imported, so put executable demonstration code under `if __name__ == "__main__":` when the file is intended for both importing and direct running. A module is not automatically a complete design; choose boundaries around responsibilities and keep dependencies understandable.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The module exposes clean_label; app imports the module and calls that public function. The import does not copy source text into app, and the guarded-main convention prevents demo code from running during import.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A Python module provides a focused interface that another module imports and uses.

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Create a `numbers_tools.py` module with one function that returns the average of a non-empty list. Import it from a separate script and write down the function's input, output, and assumption.
success_checks: The function is defined in the imported module.
The caller uses the module-qualified name and receives a value.
The interface documents the non-empty-list assumption.

items.prompt: What is a useful reason to split a program into modules?

choices.text: To separate responsibilities and limit dependencies

items.prompt: Why use an `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard?

choices.text: To prevent functions from being defined
To keep direct-run demo code from executing during import
To convert a module into JSON

items.prompt: What should an interface communicate?

choices.text: Inputs, outputs, names, and important assumptions

revision_notes: Modules group related definitions.
A small public interface reduces coupling.
Guard direct-run demonstrations so imports remain predictable.

topics.title: Use comprehensions and expressive iteration
topics.description: Comprehensions provide a compact way to create a collection from an iterable.

lesson.title: Use comprehensions and expressive iteration
objectives: Build list and dictionary comprehensions with a clear condition.
Choose a comprehension or a normal loop based on readability.
Avoid hiding complicated side effects inside a comprehension.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Comprehensions provide a compact way to create a collection from an iterable. A list comprehension has an expression, a `for` clause, and optional `if` filter. A dictionary comprehension creates key-value pairs. They are useful when the transformation is short and each input is handled independently. A normal loop is often clearer when several statements, error handling, logging, or side effects are needed. Intermediate programmers should value readability more than cleverness: a one-line expression that requires decoding is not necessarily better code. Comprehensions iterate in the same order as their source and create a new collection. They do not mutate the original list unless the expression calls a mutating operation, which is usually a design smell. Name the source and result clearly and test the empty-input case.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The dictionary comprehension filters key-value pairs while preserving their values. The list comprehension then transforms the surviving names. Both results are new collections; the original scores mapping is unchanged.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A source collection flows through a filter or transformation to produce a new collection.
blocks.content: source collection  →  filter/transform expression  →  new collection

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Rewrite a loop that selects even numbers and squares them as a list comprehension. Then write one example where a normal loop is clearer because it needs two statements.
success_checks: The comprehension includes the correct filter.
The original source collection remains unchanged.
The learner can explain when a loop is more readable.

items.prompt: What does a list comprehension normally create?
Which situation usually favors a normal loop?

choices.text: Several statements or important side effects
Filtering one list by one condition
Creating a small list of labels

items.prompt: What does the `if` clause in a comprehension do?

choices.text: It filters which source items produce results
It changes a list into a tuple

revision_notes: Comprehensions express short collection transformations.
Filters and expressions should remain easy to read.
Use loops when multi-step behavior would be obscured.

topics.title: Work with iterators, generators, and lazy data
topics.description: An iterable can provide values one at a time, while an iterator keeps iteration state and supplies the next value through `__next__`.

lesson.title: Work with iterators, generators, and lazy data
objectives: Distinguish an iterable, iterator, and generator.
Write a generator function using `yield`.
Explain why lazy evaluation can reduce memory use and change when errors occur.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: An iterable can provide values one at a time, while an iterator keeps iteration state and supplies the next value through `__next__`. A generator function is a convenient way to create an iterator: calling it returns a generator object, and each `yield` pauses the function until the next value is requested. This lazy behavior means a large sequence does not need to be stored in memory all at once. It also means the body runs during iteration, not when the generator function is called. A generator can be consumed only once unless it is recreated. Use generators for pipelines such as reading, filtering, and transforming records. Be explicit about whether a function returns a reusable list or a one-pass stream. Lazy code is powerful, but debugging and repeated access may be easier after materialising a small result with `list()`.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: Calling squares creates a generator without running its loop. `next` consumes the first value, and converting the remaining generator to a list consumes the rest. The first zero is therefore not repeated.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A generator pauses at each yield and resumes only when the next value is requested.
blocks.content: request next value  →  generator resumes  →  yield value  →  pause

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Write a generator `positive_numbers(values)` that yields only positive values. Demonstrate one `next()` call followed by consuming the rest, and explain why the first value is absent from the remaining list.
success_checks: The function uses `yield` rather than building a result list.
The generator filters values correctly.
The learner explains one-pass consumption.

items.prompt: What does `yield` do in a generator function?

choices.text: Pauses and provides a value to the caller

items.prompt: When does most generator body code execute?

choices.text: When values are requested during iteration

items.prompt: What is a common property of a consumed generator?

revision_notes: Iterables can produce values; iterators keep progress.
Generators provide lazy one-pass sequences.
Materialise data deliberately when reuse or inspection is needed.

modules.title: Model behavior and contracts
modules.description: Use classes, composition, protocols, and type-aware validation to express robust designs.

topics.title: Model data with classes, dataclasses, and methods
topics.description: A class defines a type that combines state and behavior.

lesson.title: Model data with classes, dataclasses, and methods
objectives: Define a class with an initializer and an instance method.
Use a dataclass for a small record-like model.
Choose object state and behavior that preserve useful invariants.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A class defines a type that combines state and behavior. An instance stores its own attributes, while methods describe operations on that state. The `__init__` method establishes a valid starting object. For simple records, `dataclasses.dataclass` can generate an initializer and useful representations while keeping the definition readable. A model should protect its invariants through methods or validation rather than allowing every caller to make arbitrary changes. For example, a reading item can reject a blank title and expose a method to change availability. Class design is not about making every value private or creating deep inheritance trees. Prefer a small, cohesive class with clear responsibilities. Use type annotations to communicate intended values, but remember that normal Python does not enforce annotations at runtime.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The dataclass supplies a readable constructor. The borrow method checks the state before changing it and reports whether the transition occurred. A second borrow would return False because the invariant prevents borrowing an unavailable item.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: An object receives an operation request, checks its state, and performs a valid state transition.
blocks.content: object state + method request  →  validated transition  →  new state

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Create a dataclass `Task` with a title and completed flag. Add a `complete()` method that changes the flag only once and returns whether it changed.
success_checks: The dataclass has typed fields and a useful default.
The method enforces a sensible state transition.
Repeated completion does not report a second change.

items.prompt: What is a method?

choices.text: A function associated with a class or instance

items.prompt: What does `@dataclass` help provide?

choices.text: A guarantee that inputs are valid

items.prompt: Why should a class protect invariants?

choices.text: To keep objects in meaningful valid states

revision_notes: Classes combine related state and behavior.
Dataclasses reduce boilerplate for record-like models.
Methods can enforce valid state transitions.

topics.title: Use inheritance carefully and prefer composition
topics.description: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse or specialise a base class, but it also couples the child to the parent's behavior and assumptions.

lesson.title: Use inheritance carefully and prefer composition
objectives: Explain the difference between an is-a and has-a relationship.
Use a small protocol or composed object to vary behavior.
Identify when inheritance would create a fragile hierarchy.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse or specialise a base class, but it also couples the child to the parent's behavior and assumptions. Use inheritance when the subtype truly satisfies the base type's contract: every place that accepts the base should be able to use the subtype safely. Composition means one object contains another object and delegates part of its work. It often makes variation easier because components can be replaced without changing the owning class. Python's structural typing tools, including `Protocol`, can describe the behavior a collaborator needs without requiring a shared ancestor. Keep examples small and avoid inheritance only to reuse a few lines. Clear composition and dependency injection make testing easier because a fake collaborator can be supplied. Good design is about stable contracts, not the number of classes.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: Label has a formatter rather than inheriting from one specific formatter. Any object with the required format method can be supplied, which keeps the owner loosely coupled and easy to test.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A composing object delegates to a collaborator that satisfies a small behavioral contract.
blocks.content: owner object  →  collaborator contract  →  interchangeable behavior

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Define a `Clock` protocol with `now()`. Compose a `Reminder` with a clock and test it using a small fake clock rather than the real time.
success_checks: The protocol states only the behavior the owner needs.
The owner receives its collaborator through the constructor.
A fake collaborator can be used without changing Reminder.

items.prompt: What does composition mean in object design?

choices.text: An object contains or delegates to another object
Every class must inherit from object twice

items.prompt: When is inheritance most appropriate?

choices.text: When the subtype satisfies the base contract
Whenever two classes share one line

items.prompt: What does a Protocol describe?

choices.text: Required behavior a compatible object provides

revision_notes: Inheritance creates coupling to a base contract.
Composition delegates behavior to replaceable collaborators.
Small protocols communicate required behavior clearly.

topics.title: Add type hints and validate contracts
topics.description: Type hints make intended interfaces visible to readers, editors, and static analysis tools.

lesson.title: Add type hints and validate contracts
objectives: Annotate function parameters and return values.
Use Optional-style types to represent absence explicitly.
Distinguish documentation hints from runtime validation.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Type hints make intended interfaces visible to readers, editors, and static analysis tools. They do not normally validate values at runtime, so a program that accepts external input still needs explicit checks. Annotate parameters and return types at public boundaries, especially when a value may be absent. In modern Python, `str | None` expresses either a string or `None`, while `list[int]` describes a list of integers. Keep annotations honest: do not claim an integer when a function can return a string error. Type narrowing often follows a check such as `if result is None`. Runtime validation belongs at boundaries where untrusted or loosely typed data enters the system. Type hints and validation complement each other: hints communicate the intended contract, and checks enforce the parts that must hold while the program runs.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The annotation says the function accepts text and returns either a non-negative integer or None. The implementation still performs runtime conversion and range validation because annotations alone do not enforce the contract.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: External text crosses a boundary and is validated before the function returns a typed success value or an explicit absence.
blocks.content: external text  →  conversion + validation  →  int or None

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Annotate and implement `parse_percentage(text)` returning a float from 0 to 100 or None. Test whitespace, a decimal, an out-of-range number, and invalid text.
success_checks: The return annotation represents possible absence.
Conversion errors and range errors are handled explicitly.
The tests cover valid and invalid boundary cases.

items.prompt: What do type hints primarily provide?

choices.text: Communicated intent for readers and tools
Automatic validation of all runtime data

items.prompt: What does `int | None` express?

choices.text: An integer or the absence value None

items.prompt: Where should input validation usually occur?

choices.text: At boundaries where external or loose data enters

revision_notes: Type hints document intended contracts.
Runtime checks are still required for uncertain input.
Represent absence explicitly and narrow it before use.

modules.title: Work with files and resources
modules.description: Persist structured data, manage resources safely, and define meaningful failure behavior.

topics.title: Read and write text files safely with pathlib
topics.description: File access is an external boundary: a path may not exist, permissions may differ, and text encoding matters.

lesson.title: Read and write text files safely with pathlib
objectives: Use `pathlib.Path` for portable path operations.
Read and write UTF-8 text with a context-managed API.
Handle missing files without hiding unrelated failures.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: File access is an external boundary: a path may not exist, permissions may differ, and text encoding matters. `pathlib.Path` provides readable operations such as `read_text`, `write_text`, and `/` for joining paths. Specify UTF-8 when the data is text and keep the scope of error handling narrow. Catch `FileNotFoundError` when a missing file is an expected situation, but do not catch every exception and silently discard evidence of a bug. For larger files, iterate over `Path.open()` rather than loading all content at once. A `with` statement closes the file even when an error occurs. This lesson uses a temporary directory in the example so it does not alter a learner's personal files. Production programs should decide clearly where data belongs and what failure message is safe to show.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

with TemporaryDirectory() as folder:
    path = Path(folder) / "notes.txt"
    path.write_text("first line\nsecond line\n", encoding="utf-8")
    lines = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()
    print(len(lines), lines[0])
blocks.explanation: The temporary directory is created for the example and removed afterward. Path joins the directory and filename, while explicit UTF-8 keeps text handling predictable.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A Path identifies a file, which is written and read using an explicit text encoding.
blocks.content: Path  →  UTF-8 file  →  lines in memory

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Use a temporary directory to write three lines, read them with `Path.open()` iteration, and count non-empty lines. Add a narrow missing-file message.
success_checks: Paths are joined with Path operations.
The file is opened with UTF-8 and closed safely.
Missing-file handling is narrow and does not catch every error.

items.prompt: Why specify an encoding for text files?
What does a `with` statement help ensure for an opened file?

choices.text: The file is closed after the block

items.prompt: Which exception specifically represents a missing path?

revision_notes: Pathlib expresses filesystem paths portably.
Use context management and explicit UTF-8.
Handle expected filesystem failures narrowly.

topics.title: Serialize structured data with JSON
topics.description: JSON is a text format for interoperable data such as objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null.

lesson.title: Serialize structured data with JSON
objectives: Convert JSON-compatible Python values to and from text.
Validate the shape of decoded data before using it.
Explain why JSON is data interchange, not arbitrary Python execution.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: JSON is a text format for interoperable data such as objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. Python's `json.dumps` serializes compatible values to text, while `json.loads` parses text back into Python values. Parsing is not enough: the text may be valid JSON but have the wrong shape, missing keys, or unexpected value types. Validate at the boundary before business logic uses the data. Avoid using `eval` to parse a data file; it can execute Python expressions and is not a safe interchange mechanism. When writing JSON for people, indentation improves readability; when writing for a machine, compact output may be smaller. Decide how absent fields and version changes will be handled, and keep personal or sensitive data out of practice files.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The record is converted to JSON text and parsed back. The shape check confirms that the top-level value is an object and tags is a list before the values are used.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: Structured Python data is serialized to JSON text, parsed, and checked before use.
blocks.content: Python values  →  JSON text  →  parse  →  shape validation

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Serialize a list of fictional tasks to JSON, parse it again, and write a function that returns False for a decoded value that is not a list of objects with string titles.
success_checks: The JSON round trip succeeds without using eval.
The decoded shape is checked before indexing.
Malformed or wrong-shaped data is rejected clearly.

items.prompt: Which function converts a Python value to JSON text?
Why validate parsed JSON shape?

choices.text: Valid JSON can still have unexpected fields or types

items.prompt: Why should `eval` not parse untrusted data?

revision_notes: JSON is a text interchange format.
Parse and validate shape at the boundary.
Never use eval as a general data parser.

topics.title: Use context managers and custom exceptions
topics.description: A context manager defines setup and cleanup around a block.

lesson.title: Use context managers and custom exceptions
objectives: Explain the resource-management role of a context manager.
Implement `__enter__` and `__exit__` for a small resource.
Raise and catch a domain-specific exception at an appropriate boundary.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A context manager defines setup and cleanup around a block. The `with` statement calls `__enter__` before the body and `__exit__` afterward, even when an exception is raised. Files use this pattern, and custom resources can use it too. A domain-specific exception gives callers a meaningful failure type without forcing them to inspect arbitrary messages. Raise an exception when a function cannot satisfy its contract, and catch it where the program can respond usefully. Do not use exceptions for ordinary branching when a normal return value is clearer. In `__exit__`, returning False allows an exception to propagate; returning True suppresses it and should be rare and intentional. Cleanup should be reliable, and error messages should avoid exposing secrets or internal paths unnecessarily.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The context manager returns the resource, and its exit method permits the domain exception to propagate. The caller catches only the expected quota failure and reports its type and safe message.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A with block acquires a resource, performs work, and always reaches its exit cleanup path.
blocks.content: with block  →  enter resource  →  work  →  exit cleanup

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Create a `TemporaryFlag` context manager that sets a Boolean on entry and resets it on exit. Raise a custom `InvalidStateError` when a transition is not allowed, and catch it in a caller.
success_checks: Entry and exit establish and clean up state.
The custom exception represents a domain failure.
The caller catches the expected exception at the response boundary.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of a context manager?

choices.text: Reliable setup and cleanup around a block

items.prompt: Why define a custom exception?

choices.text: To name a meaningful domain failure

items.prompt: What does returning False from `__exit__` normally do?

revision_notes: Context managers make cleanup explicit and reliable.
Custom exceptions communicate domain failures.
Catch expected exceptions where a useful response is possible.

modules.title: Test, debug, and integrate
modules.description: Use automated tests, responsible logging, and maintainable application boundaries.

topics.title: Test with unittest, mocks, and boundary cases
topics.description: Automated tests turn expected behavior into repeatable checks.

lesson.title: Test with unittest, mocks, and boundary cases
objectives: Write a focused unittest for a pure function.
Use a fake collaborator or mock to isolate a unit.
Choose boundary and failure cases that reveal incorrect assumptions.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Automated tests turn expected behavior into repeatable checks. A unit test should focus on one behavior and use a clear arrange, act, assert structure. Pure functions are easy to test because the same inputs produce the same outputs without external state. When a component depends on a clock, filesystem, or service, inject that dependency and supply a fake or mock in the test. Test boundaries such as zero, the first allowed value, the last allowed value, empty collections, invalid input, and repeated operations. Tests are not proof that every case is correct, but they provide a fast regression signal. Keep tests deterministic and independent: a test should not depend on another test's execution order or a live network. A failing test is evidence to investigate, not a reason to weaken the assertion.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The test runner reports a passing test without printing a result when executed normally. The assertions cover below-range, above-range, and in-range behavior.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A test arranges inputs, calls a unit, and asserts a result or expected failure.
blocks.content: arrange inputs  →  call unit  →  assert expected behavior

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Write unittest cases for a `percentage(value)` function that accepts 0 through 100 and raises ValueError otherwise. Include both boundary values, a middle value, and two invalid values.
success_checks: Tests use clear assertions and descriptive method names.
Both boundaries and invalid values are covered.
The function contract is checked without external services.

items.prompt: What makes a unit test easier to trust?

choices.text: Deterministic inputs and one focused behavior

items.prompt: Why inject a clock or service dependency?

choices.text: To replace it with a fake during tests
To make tests depend on the network

items.prompt: Which is a useful boundary test?

choices.text: The first and last allowed values plus invalid neighbors

revision_notes: Unit tests encode expected behavior.
Inject collaborators so tests stay deterministic.
Test boundaries, emptiness, repetition, and failures.

topics.title: Debug systematically and use logging responsibly
topics.description: Debugging is a reasoning process rather than random editing.

lesson.title: Debug systematically and use logging responsibly
objectives: Read a traceback from the bottom upward to find the failure context.
Add focused logging without exposing sensitive values.
Use a minimal reproduction and hypothesis-driven debugging process.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: Debugging is a reasoning process rather than random editing. Start with the traceback: the exception type and final message describe the immediate failure, while the stack frames show how execution reached it. Reproduce the issue with the smallest input that still fails. State a hypothesis, add a targeted observation or breakpoint, and change one thing at a time. The `logging` module provides levels such as DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, and ERROR; use them to record useful state transitions without printing secrets, tokens, or unnecessary personal data. Remove temporary prints or replace them with purposeful logs before delivery. A bug may be in data assumptions, control flow, timing, or a boundary contract. Once fixed, add a regression test for the smallest failing case. Good debugging leaves the program and its evidence clearer than before.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.code:
import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s:%(message)s")

def lookup(items, wanted):
    logging.info("lookup started; item_count=%d", len(items))
    for item in items:
        if item.casefold() == wanted.casefold():
            logging.info("lookup matched")
            return item
    logging.warning("lookup missed")
    return None

print(lookup(["Python", "Testing"], "python"))
blocks.explanation: The logs record counts and outcome but not sensitive input values. The function returns the matched item for the caller to print, keeping diagnostic output separate from the program's result.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: A failure is investigated with evidence, a hypothesis, a focused fix, and a regression test.
blocks.content: failure  →  traceback + logs  →  hypothesis  →  minimal fix + regression test

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Introduce a deliberate bug in a search function. Capture the traceback, reduce the input to two values, add an INFO log for the number of items, fix the comparison, and write the regression test.
success_checks: The reproduction is small and repeatable.
Logs reveal useful non-sensitive state.
The fix is protected by a regression test.

items.prompt: What is a good first step when reading a traceback?

choices.text: Inspect the exception type/message and relevant bottom frame

items.prompt: What should logs avoid?
What should follow a bug fix?

choices.text: A regression test for the failing case

revision_notes: Use traceback evidence before editing.
Log useful, non-sensitive events at appropriate levels.
Turn each fixed bug into a regression test.

topics.title: Integrate a maintainable Python application
topics.description: A maintainable application is more than a collection of advanced syntax.

lesson.title: Integrate a maintainable Python application
objectives: Combine modules, models, persistence, validation, and tests in a small design.
Explain the boundaries and failure behavior of an application.
Use a delivery checklist to review quality, privacy, and maintainability.

blocks.title: Understand the idea
blocks.body: A maintainable application is more than a collection of advanced syntax. It has boundaries: a domain model represents the problem, services coordinate use cases, persistence translates data to storage, and an entry point handles user interaction. Keep those responsibilities visible and test the domain logic without requiring a real filesystem or network. Validate external data before it enters the domain, return or raise clear failures, and log only appropriate operational information. A small application should have a README or usage note, predictable setup, automated checks, and a clear statement of limitations. Review security and privacy even for a practice project: do not collect unnecessary personal information, do not embed secrets, and do not assume local files are a database. Integration is successful when the parts work together and remain understandable to another programmer.

blocks.title: Read and predict the example
blocks.explanation: The model stores one note type, the collection coordinates adding and searching, and the caller observes a stable result. Blank input is rejected and an empty search returns no matches without accessing external systems.

blocks.title: At a glance
blocks.alt_text: An input crosses a boundary, is handled by domain objects, and produces a validated result for the caller.
blocks.content: input boundary  →  domain object/service  →  validated result

blocks.title: Try it yourself
instructions: Design a small in-memory task manager with a dataclass, a service class, validation, search, three unit tests, and a README checklist. Keep it free of accounts, network calls, and personal data.
success_checks: The design separates model and service responsibilities.
Blank input and no-match cases are safe.
Tests, usage notes, and privacy limitations are included.

items.prompt: What is a useful application boundary?

choices.text: A clear place where data is validated or responsibility changes

items.prompt: Which quality check belongs in a small project review?

choices.text: Only whether the happy path prints
Tests, failure cases, setup notes, and privacy limits
Whether code uses the most classes

items.prompt: Why keep practice applications free of unnecessary personal data?

choices.text: It reduces privacy risk and keeps the design focused
It removes the need for functions

blocks.title: Maintainable Offline Task Notebook
blocks.purpose: Build a small, tested, in-memory Python task notebook that demonstrates intermediate design, validation, persistence-format awareness, and maintainable boundaries without becoming a deployed service.
privacy_and_limits: Use fictional task text only; do not collect names, contact details, credentials, or learner identifiers.
Keep the working data in memory and use temporary files only for controlled JSON demonstrations; do not contact a network.
Python 3.10+ standard library only; no third-party packages required.
requirements: Model tasks with a dataclass or similarly clear class and a stable identifier or title.
Separate task behavior from the command-line or demonstration entry point.
Support add, complete, search, and list operations with validation for blank or duplicate titles.
Provide JSON export/import or a clearly validated JSON boundary without using eval.
Use at least five focused unit tests covering normal, empty, duplicate, invalid, and repeated-operation cases.
Use a replaceable collaborator or clear dependency boundary where it improves testing.
Include a README describing setup, usage, limitations, and privacy choices.
suggested_steps: Design the model and write pure validation/search behavior first.
Add a service or collection class with small methods and tests.
